Random forest importance with a held-out evaluation

Source: R/fs_randomforest.R
fs_randomforest.Rd

Fits a random forest on a stratified training split, scores each predictor by permutation importance, and evaluates the forest on the held-out rows. Unless you supply control$feature_select, selected holds every predictor the forest used, ordered by importance, and you choose where to cut the list.

Usage

fs_randomforest(
  data,
  target,
  task = c("classification", "regression"),
  control = list(),
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  n_cores = 1L
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame or data.table with at least one row and one column, holding the target and the candidate predictors (every other column). Column names must be unique and non-empty, and predictors may not contain infinite values. Date columns are converted to numeric before modeling.

target

Name of the target column of data, as a single string (a column index is not accepted). For classification the target is coerced with as.factor(), an ordered factor is treated as unordered, and at least two levels must remain. For regression it is coerced with as.numeric(), a factor through its labels (as.numeric(as.character(y))) and never its internal level codes, and an infinite value is an error. Either way, rows whose target is NA after coercion are dropped with a warning.

task

"classification" (the default) or "regression", matched with match.arg(). The task is not inferred from the target. If you leave task at its default and the target is numeric, a warning says that every distinct value will become a class.

control

List of method-specific options. Every accepted entry and its default is listed under "The control list" in Details. Default list(), meaning all defaults.

seed

Optional single whole number within the range of an R integer; fractional or out-of-range values are an error. The seed applies for the duration of the call and the previous RNG state is restored on exit. With more than one worker it is also passed to parallel::clusterSetRNGStream(), and it is then the only way to make the run reproducible. Default NULL: the RNG is never seeded unless you ask.

verbose

Logical. If TRUE, print the split sizes, how many predictors the hook kept, the tree and worker counts, and a note when AUC is skipped because 'pROC' is missing. Default FALSE.

n_cores

Number of workers used to grow the forest, a whole number >= 1. Default 1L (sequential; no cluster is created). Capped at the detected core count and at control$ntree. An effective value above 1 needs the suggested packages 'foreach' and 'doParallel', and leaves details$oob empty (see Details).

Value

An object of class fs_result with:

selected

Character vector. With control$feature_select, the predictors the hook kept; otherwise every predictor that reached the forest. Ordered by decreasing importance when importance was computed.

scores

Named numeric vector of permutation importance from randomForest::importance(type = 1): mean decrease in accuracy for classification, mean increase in MSE for regression (randomForest names that column with a percent sign, but it is not a percentage). Scaled or not according to control$scale_importance. NULL when control$importance = FALSE.

method

"randomforest".

task

"classification" or "regression", echoing the task argument.

model

The fitted randomForest object, or the result of randomForest::combine() when more than one worker was used.

details

A list with:

  • metrics: held-out metrics, a named list with accuracy, kappa, and auc for classification, or RMSE, MAE, and R2 for regression.

  • predictions: test-set predictions.

  • probabilities: test-set class probability matrix (classification only; NULL if predict() cannot produce one).

  • importance: data.frame with columns feature and importance, sorted descending; NULL when control$importance = FALSE.

  • confusion: Observed x Predicted table (classification only).

  • oob: out-of-bag accuracy or RMSE; NULL when trained in parallel or switched off.

  • feature_names: the predictors the forest used.

  • train_index: integer training rows of the cleaned and optionally downsampled data.

  • test_data: the held-out rows when control$return_test_data = TRUE, NULL otherwise.

  • control: the merged control list.

  • n_features: candidate predictors after cleaning and before selection.

call

The matched call.

Details

A random forest averages many decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample of the training rows with a random subset of predictors tried at each split. Forests take any mix of numeric, factor, character, and Date predictors and need no scaling, so fs_randomforest() is a reasonable default when the feature types are messy. Permutation importance is the drop in out-of-bag accuracy (or rise in out-of-bag MSE) when one predictor's values are shuffled. It tends to favor predictors with many distinct values and to split credit between correlated predictors, so treat close scores as ties.

The honest performance estimate is details$metrics, computed on rows the forest and the selection hook never saw (control$preprocess does see them; see "What sees the held-out rows"). The Validation and leakage article lists which numbers in each featR result are held out and which are optimistic.

Order of operations

  1. control$preprocess runs on the full table.

  2. Date columns become numeric, and the target is coerced and cleaned (see target).

  3. If control$sample_size is set, the table is downsampled.

  4. The rows are split into training and test sets, stratified on the target, with control$train_ratio of them used for training.

  5. control$feature_select runs on the training rows.

  6. Character predictors become factors, unused factor levels are dropped, and the test factors are re-leveled to the training levels.

  7. Near-zero-variance predictors are removed, judged on the training rows.

  8. Missing predictor values are imputed with values learned on the training rows.

  9. The forest is grown, on n_cores workers.

  10. The forest predicts the test rows, and permutation importance is read from it.

Because near-zero-variance removal comes after the hook, details$feature_names (the predictors the forest used) can be a subset of selected.

The control list

Every accepted entry, with its default:

  • train_ratio = 0.75: training proportion of the stratified split, strictly between 0 and 1.

  • sample_size = NULL: optional whole number. When set, the data is downsampled to about this many rows before the split, proportionally within each class for classification and uniformly at random for regression. Values above the available row count are capped. NULL keeps every row.

  • ntree = 500: number of trees, a whole number >= 1.

  • importance = TRUE: compute permutation importance. When FALSE, scores and details$importance are NULL and selected keeps column order.

  • scale_importance = TRUE: passed as scale to randomForest::importance(), which divides each permutation importance by its standard error over trees. Set FALSE for the raw importance. With more than one worker the standard error is pooled across the sub-forests, so scaled scores do not depend on n_cores.

  • mtry = NULL: predictors tried at each split. NULL means floor(sqrt(p)) for classification and floor(p / 3) for regression. Any value, supplied or derived, is clamped to [1, p], where p counts the predictors left after the hook and near-zero-variance removal.

  • nodesize = NULL: minimum size of terminal nodes, a whole number >= 1. NULL keeps the randomForest default (1 for classification, 5 for regression).

  • maxnodes = NULL: maximum number of terminal nodes per tree, a whole number >= 2, or NULL for no limit.

  • sampsize = NULL: rows drawn to grow each tree, passed to randomForest. Regression takes a single number (a vector is an error); classification also accepts one number per class. Entries must be whole numbers >= 1. A single value is clamped to the training row count. A per-class (or, with strata, per-stratum) vector has each entry clamped to that class's (stratum's) count in the training rows, with a warning, because randomForest refuses larger entries and you cannot know the training split in advance. An NA entry becomes the full training size when replace = TRUE and ceiling(0.632 * n) otherwise, and is then clamped the same way.

  • classwt = NULL: class priors for classification, passed to randomForest unchanged and unvalidated.

  • strata = NULL: name of a column of data to stratify the per-tree sampling on (used with sampsize). Its values are read from the training rows so they line up with the rows the forest is grown on. Passing the values as a vector is an error, because the training rows are chosen inside the function. The column must not contain NA, and it stays in the model as a predictor unless you remove it.

  • replace = TRUE: sample rows with replacement when growing each tree.

  • preprocess = NULL: a function dt -> dt applied to the full data before the split. It must return a data.frame or data.table that still contains the target. See "What sees the held-out rows" below.

  • feature_select = NULL: a function dt -> dt that runs on the training rows only. It must keep the target and may only subset and reorder existing columns, because the same columns are then taken from the test rows. Put feature engineering in preprocess.

  • impute = TRUE: replace missing predictor values with the median (numeric) or the most frequent value (factor, character, logical), learned on the training rows and applied to both splits.

  • drop_zerovar = TRUE: remove near-zero-variance predictors with caret::nearZeroVar(), using the training rows only. With FALSE, training rows in which every predictor is constant are an error, since the trees have nothing to split on.

  • oob = TRUE: report out-of-bag metrics in details$oob (accuracy for classification, RMSE for regression). They are optimistic after a supervised hook and unavailable after parallel training; see below.

  • return_test_data = FALSE: when TRUE, the held-out rows are returned in details$test_data.

  • positive_class = NULL: level treated as the positive class for binary AUC. NULL means the second factor level. A string that does not name a level of the cleaned target is an error.

Unknown entries are an error, so typos and arguments that moved out of control (seed, n_cores, and split_ratio, now train_ratio) fail loudly.

What sees the held-out rows

control$feature_select runs after the split on the training rows only, so a hook that looks at the target does not leak the test rows into details$metrics.

The out-of-bag metrics in details$oob do not get that protection. The forest is grown on the same training rows the hook selected on, so an out-of-bag row was left out of some trees but was still used for the selection. With a hook that consults the target, details$oob is optimistic, and on pure noise it can read well above chance.

control$preprocess runs on the full data by design. Any quantity it learns from other rows, such as an imputation value, a scaling constant, or anything computed from the target, includes the test rows and will flatter details$metrics. Keep it to row-wise transformations. Downsampling with control$sample_size also happens before the split, which is why details$train_index indexes the cleaned and downsampled table rather than the rows of data.

When more than one worker is used (n_cores after the caps), the sub-forests are merged with randomForest::combine(), which drops the out-of-bag error structures (err.rate, mse, confusion). details$oob is then NULL, with a warning if control$oob = TRUE. details$metrics is unaffected; use n_cores = 1 to get the out-of-bag numbers.

Factor levels and missing values

Factor predictors carry only the levels seen in the training rows. A test value unseen in training becomes NA and is imputed when control$impute = TRUE. With control$impute = FALSE, any NA left in a predictor reaches randomForest, which fails on it.

Metrics

Classification reports accuracy, kappa, and auc on the held-out rows. kappa is Cohen's kappa from the held-out confusion table, NA when chance agreement is 1. auc is filled in only when the target has exactly two levels and the suggested package 'pROC' is installed. It is NA for every multi-class fit, and also (with a warning) when the held-out rows contain only one of the two classes.

For a binary target, the positive class (whose predicted probability is scored) is control$positive_class or, by default, the second factor level after unused levels are dropped. fs_mars() uses the first level. ROC AUC is the same whichever class is called positive, so auc does not depend on this choice, but class-specific quantities such as fs_mars()'s PR AUC or sensitivity are not directly comparable with anything computed here.

Regression reports RMSE, MAE, and R2 on the held-out rows. R2 is 1 - SSE/SST, so it can be negative; it is not the squared correlation that fs_mars() reports. It is NA when the held-out target has no variance, including variance that is only floating-point round-off relative to the target's magnitude.

See also

The Regularization and embedded importance guide, which runs this function on a worked example.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("randomForest", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("caret", quietly = TRUE)) {
  res <- fs_randomforest(
    iris,
    target = "Species",
    task = "classification",
    control = list(ntree = 100),
    seed = 42
  )
  # every predictor, in decreasing order of importance
  print(res$selected)
  print(res$scores)
  print(res$details$metrics)
}
#> [1] "Petal.Length" "Petal.Width"  "Sepal.Length" "Sepal.Width" 
#> Petal.Length  Petal.Width Sepal.Length  Sepal.Width 
#>    15.409812    12.423520     3.745021     1.804016 
#> $accuracy
#> [1] 0.9444444
#> 
#> $kappa
#> [1] 0.9166667
#> 
#> $auc
#> [1] NA
#> 
# }
